solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Each one consuming steak and kidney?

indicators.note: consuming means eating up, so the card word swallows the pastry dish

parts.note: an ace is the one in a pack of cards
steak and kidney is a classic British pie filling, standing for the pie itself

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether each diner gets a steak and kidney pie of their own.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words mean for every single one, as in 'a pound apiece'.

clue.text: Request Head should be removed from duty

indicators.note: tells us to drop the opening letter of the word meaning duty

parts.note: a duty is a task you must perform

explanation.surface: A demand that a boss be relieved of his responsibilities.
explanation.definitionFit: To request something is to ask for it; a direct synonym.

clue.text: Irritating Cockney's after a lift?

indicators.note: a Cockney speaker famously drops the opening H of words

parts.note: someone hitching is thumbing a ride, seeking a lift

explanation.surface: A Cockney grumbles that waiting for a lift is wearing on him.
explanation.walkthrough: Cockneys, the working-class Londoners of East London, traditionally drop their H's, so 'Cockney's' removes the H.
explanation.definitionFit: Something itching makes you want to scratch, so it is annoying or irritating.

clue.text: Do a "not so hot" dog please!

definitions.text: Do a "not so hot" dog please!

parts.words: Do a "not so hot" dog please!
parts.note: the idiom for doing well enough is read literally as a request to hold back the hot condiment on a frankfurter

explanation.surface: A customer at a hot-dog stand asks for a milder sausage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Do' is the idiom's sense of succeeding; the rest asks for no spicy yellow sauce on the sausage.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means to be good enough, to succeed or 'do', and literally means leaving off the condiment.

clue.text: Modify, once more, wind instrument with it

parts.note: a reed is a simple wind instrument, like a pipe

explanation.surface: An instruction to rework a piece written for a woodwind player.
explanation.definitionFit: To edit again means to revise or modify a text a second time.

clue.text: Horse-riding in Times Square unusual

indicators.note: unusual signals that these letters come out in an unexpected order

explanation.surface: Horseback riders in the middle of Times Square would be an odd sight.
explanation.definitionFit: Equestrian sport is the skill or practice of riding horses.

clue.text: Look proud, like stock folk hero, last of all

indicators.note: the final letter of all five words before it is taken

explanation.surface: An invitation to admire a proud, archetypal folk hero.
explanation.walkthrough: A dekko is British slang for a quick look.
explanation.definitionFit: British slang for a quick glance, from Hindi, as in 'have a dekko'.

clue.text: Allegretto tempo lends covers something symbolic?

indicators.note: the phrase covers, or conceals, the answer within its letters

explanation.surface: A musical marking of moderate speed adds something meaningful to a piece.
explanation.definitionFit: A carved post bearing emblems of a clan or tribe is literally a symbolic object.

clue.text: Highland peak in W African state

parts.note: ben is the Scottish word for a mountain, as in Ben Nevis

explanation.surface: A Scottish mountain turns up in a West African country.
explanation.definitionFit: Benin is a nation on the Gulf of Guinea in West Africa.

clue.text: Pass on, or give up, the water container

parts.note: to kick a habit is to give it up
a bucket holds water

explanation.surface: A choice about passing a pail of water along or abandoning it.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are euphemisms for dying; the idiom is a jocular way to say pass away.

clue.text: Greek character flops in shows

indicators.note: the phrase shows, or displays, the answer within its letters

explanation.surface: An actor from Greece keeps appearing in theatrical failures.
explanation.definitionFit: Psi is the twenty-third letter of the Greek alphabet.

clue.text: Nearly all clean gone after getting bought

indicators.note: keep all of the word for clean except its last letter

parts.note: pure means clean, unsullied
to chase is to go after, so gone after is chased

explanation.surface: Almost every cleaning product was snapped up once it went on sale.
explanation.definitionFit: Purchased and bought are both past forms meaning acquired for money.

clue.text: Greetings to Royal Marines in spell of bad weather

parts.note: hails are greetings or salutes

explanation.surface: Commandos are welcomed during a spell of poor weather.
explanation.definitionFit: A storm of falling ice pellets is a burst of foul weather.

clue.text: Rule émigré out of order

indicators.note: out of order says the letters are not in their proper sequence

explanation.surface: A judgement that an exile's conduct was improper.
explanation.definitionFit: A regime is a system of government or rule.

clue.text: Rubbish to put in fancy hollow?

parts.note: grot is British slang for rubbish or junk

explanation.surface: Instructions for dumping junk inside an ornate cavity.
explanation.definitionFit: A grotto is a small cave, often an ornamental one in a garden.

clue.text: Chuckled: "Peg needs attention"

parts.note: a tee is the peg a golfer sets the ball on
heed means attention or notice

explanation.surface: Someone laughed at a remark that a woman named Peg needs looking after.
explanation.definitionFit: To tee-hee is to giggle or titter, a past-tense verb of laughing.

clue.text: Unrestrained in speech, getting Oscar?

indicators.note: in speech says the word is heard spoken rather than written

parts.note: wild means unrestrained

explanation.surface: An actor goes wild in his acceptance speech for an Academy Award.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Oscar' suggests the film award; it is the Irish writer Oscar Wilde.
explanation.definitionFit: Oscar Wilde, the Irish playwright, is an example of someone called Oscar.

clue.text: Port and Irish ham cooked with nothing in

indicators.note: in places the round letter for nothing inside the rearranged letters
cooked signals the letters are prepared in a new arrangement

parts.note: O looks like zero, nothing

explanation.surface: A recipe for Irish ham with nothing added.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cooked' turns IRISH HAM into HIRSHIMA, and O goes in after HIR.
explanation.definitionFit: Hiroshima is a Japanese city with a major seaport.

clue.text: Quarrel leading to arrest?

definitions.meaning: an argument or clash with someone
to run someone in is to take them into custody, so this is what precedes it

explanation.definitionFit: A run-in is a quarrel, and to run in a suspect is slang for arresting them.

clue.text: Wool supplier in Uzbekistan's capital called out

indicators.note: called out says the letter is heard as spoken
the capital, or first letter, of the country's name

explanation.surface: A sheep farmer in Tashkent is named publicly.
explanation.definitionFit: A female sheep provides wool, so it supplies the fleece.

clue.text: DVD insurer, say, makes for motorists occasionally

indicators.note: makes says these letters are made into something new

explanation.surface: An insurance company's video explains what sort of drivers it covers.
explanation.definitionFit: Sunday drivers are people who motor only at leisure, now and then, often slowly.

clue.text: Quiet English female

parts.note: sh is a call for quiet

explanation.surface: A description of a reserved English woman.
explanation.definitionFit: The pronoun refers to a woman or female animal; used as a noun it means a female.

clue.text: Strip in French appearing in Dandy?

indicators.note: appearing in places the French word inside the word for a dandy

parts.note: a dude is a dandy, a man very fond of clothes
en is French for in

explanation.surface: A stripper turns up in The Dandy, a British children's comic.
explanation.definitionFit: To denude is to strip bare, to remove the covering.

clue.text: Small slander, for example, turning to smear

parts.note: mud, as in mud-slinging, is slander

indicators.note: turning says the abbreviation is read backwards

explanation.surface: Petty slander soon turns into a full smear campaign.
explanation.definitionFit: A smudge is a blurred mark, the same as a smear.
